reading.body:
The largest AI deals in life sciences are cloud consumption commitments, not software purchases. Merck and Google Cloud announced a multiyear collaboration valued at up to $1 billion to deploy agentic AI across Merck's global business.

Hyperscalers sell drugmakers a whole platform: infrastructure, data platforms, model access and agent building tools. Multiyear agreements bundle cloud migration, data modernisation and AI development together, which is why headline values reach hundreds of millions or more. The Merck figure is an up-to number, so it indicates ambition rather than committed spend.

For AI specifically, the constraint this reveals is organisational rather than computational. The value depends on the work inside the deal, migrating and governing data, building agents for specific workflows, and changing processes so they are used. A billion dollars buys access to compute and tools, but it does not buy the data readiness or the process change that decide whether agents get used.

The data covers one announced partnership and the general shape of hyperscaler agreements. It does not say how much of the Merck value is cloud consumption versus AI work, what milestones release payment, or whether any of it has been spent.

A hyperscaler is a company that builds and runs very large networks of data centers to provide computing power and online services at massive scale, such as Amazon Web Services, Google, or Meta.

An AI system that takes a goal, breaks it into steps, and carries those steps out using tools, rather than answering a single question and stopping. The defining trait is initiative between instructions: the agent decides what to do next.

siblings.name: Governing AI in a Regulated Company

explainer:
Hyperscalers, the largest cloud providers, sell drugmakers the infrastructure, data platforms, model access and agent building tools needed to run AI across a business. Multiyear agreements often bundle cloud migration, data modernisation and AI development, which is why headline values can reach hundreds of millions or more.

The value depends on the work inside the deal: migrating and governing data, building agents for specific workflows, and changing processes so they are used. Up-to values usually depend on consumption and milestones, so they indicate ambition rather than spend.

What these deals usually contain

The public announcements sound alike, but the substance varies. Most combine four things: a commitment to run a share of the company's workloads on one cloud, access to that cloud's AI models and tools, joint engineering teams that build specific applications, and co-marketing. Some add dedicated computing capacity for drug discovery or imaging, which is the part that is hardest to buy on the open market. A few include revenue sharing or minimum spend commitments that are not disclosed.

Why pharma signs them

A large pharmaceutical company has data in hundreds of systems across research, trials, manufacturing and commercial teams. A cloud partner offers one place to put it, security certifications the company would otherwise have to prove itself, and models that are updated without an internal team maintaining them. For companies that are not technology businesses, buying this capability is faster than building it.

What to watch for

The risks are concentration and lock in. Data formats, agent frameworks and validated pipelines built on one provider are expensive to move. Regulators also expect the company, not the cloud provider, to answer for data integrity and patient privacy, so the contract has to spell out audit rights, data residency, model change notification and what happens to validated systems when the provider updates a model. Companies with the most leverage keep at least one critical workload portable and negotiate for it.
